passage: The waiting room outside the college sports physio smelled of antiseptic and old mats. Leela sat with her knee strapped, staring at the trophy cabinet. Two months ago she'd been picked for the state hockey camp, the first step toward the national team she'd trained for since she was twelve. Then the tackle. The torn ligament. The doctor's words that morning had been careful and kind: she'd walk and run again, but competitive hockey at that level probably wasn't coming back. Her teammate Gopika came in, sat down, and handed her a bottle of water. Leela said, "I don't even know who I am if I'm not that." Gopika didn't try to fix it. She just said, "You're still you," and stayed until the physio called her name.

qa.q: Where did Leela sit with her knee strapped?
qa.a: In the waiting room outside the college sports physio.

qa.q: What does Leela mean when she says she doesn't know who she is anymore?
qa.a: She is grieving not just the injury but the future and identity she had built around hockey since she was twelve.

qa.q: Why was Gopika's quiet presence helpful?
qa.a: She didn't rush to fix or minimise the loss, which let Leela feel her sorrow without being alone. 🤍

qa.q: How might the loss feel different for Gopika, who is still on the team?
qa.a: She may feel sad for her friend and perhaps a little guilty that her own path continues while Leela's has changed.

grounding: Shows a young adult grieving the loss of an idealised future after a career-ending injury.

passage:
Dear Bhaiya,

You asked why I've been quiet on calls. Meera and I broke up. Four years. It was mutual, which somehow makes it worse. Nobody did anything wrong. We just wanted different cities, different lives.

I keep reaching for my phone to tell her small things, like the new chai place near the office, and then I remember. I walk past our bench in the park and feel hollow. I had a whole future in my head: the flat, the dog, Sunday lunches with both families. Now that future is just gone, and I didn't know you could grieve something that never actually happened.

I'm okay, mostly. Going to work, eating. Just sad in a deep, slow way.

Come home for Diwali?

Tanvir

qa.q: How long were Tanvir and Meera together?
qa.a: Four years.

qa.q: Why does Tanvir feel the grief is for more than Meera herself?
qa.a: Tanvir is mourning the imagined future they had planned together, the flat, the dog, the family lunches, which now won't happen.

qa.q: What could Bhaiya do in reply?
qa.a: Call Tanvir, listen without trying to fix it, and make a plan to be together at Diwali as Tanvir asked. 🫂

qa.q: How might Meera be experiencing the same breakup?
qa.a: Since it was mutual, she may also be grieving the future they shared, even though she agreed it had to end.

grounding: A young adult writes about the deep sorrow of losing a long relationship and the future they had imagined.

passage: Dhruv rubbed his face with both hands. "Amandeep, you know how long I prepared for the army. Since Class 9. Morning runs, pushups on the terrace, the medical, the written test, the interview. I thought I'd done well. Yesterday the final list came out. My name wasn't there. And I'm over the age limit for trying again. That's it. Done. I didn't cry in front of Mummy. I went to the ground where I used to run and sat there till it got dark. It's not just the job, you know? It's the picture I carried of myself in uniform, making Papa proud. That picture's just... gone. I don't know what I want now. I'm not asking you to fix it. I just needed to say it out loud to someone."

qa.q: Since which class had Dhruv been preparing for the army?
qa.a: Since Class 9.

qa.q: Why did Dhruv go to the ground and sit there until dark?
qa.a: He was grieving deeply and needed a place to feel the loss privately, away from his mother.

qa.q: How could Amandeep best respond right now?
qa.a: By listening and staying with him instead of offering quick solutions, as Dhruv asked, and checking in over the next days.

qa.q: What would change if Dhruv's father were in the room hearing this?
qa.a: Dhruv might feel he had failed him, or he might realise his father cares about him more than the uniform.

grounding: A young man tells a friend about the sorrow of losing the future he had long imagined for himself.

passage: I'm Omkar, Maria's younger brother. Last month her engagement to the man she'd been with since college ended. Five years. She didn't explain much to us, only that it was over and nobody did anything terrible. At first she kept going to work like normal. Then I noticed she'd stopped singing in the shower, which she has done my whole life. On Sunday she sat on the balcony with the box of wedding cards they had already printed and folded them into little boats, one by one, without speaking. I sat with her. I don't know if she was angry or just very sad. When the box was empty, she said, 'I had the whole house planned. Even the curtains.' Then she went in and made us both tea.

qa.q: How long had Maria been with the man?
qa.a: Five years, since college.

qa.q: What might folding the wedding cards into boats suggest about Maria's feelings?
qa.a: It may suggest she was quietly grieving the future she had planned and letting it go slowly, though Omkar can't be sure.

qa.q: How could Omkar keep supporting his sister?
qa.a: He can keep sitting with her without pushing for explanations, and if the sadness stays heavy, gently suggest family time or a counsellor.

qa.q: How might this loss feel different for Maria than for her family?
qa.a: For her it is the loss of a whole imagined life, down to the curtains; the family sees the breakup but not all the plans that ended with it.

grounding: Shows a young adult grieving the end of a long relationship and the future she had imagined, seen by her brother.

passage:
Week one: The doctor's words were gentle, but Jomon, twenty-one, heard only that he would never play at that level again. At home he turned his team jersey inside out and stuffed it at the back of the cupboard. When Ishita called, he said he was fine and hung up.
Week three: Ishita came anyway, with banana chips. He talked for an hour about the trials he'd miss, the coach who had believed in him, the future he had drawn since he was twelve. He cried, which he hadn't done in years. She just listened.
Week six: He went to the ground as a spectator for the first time. It hurt to watch. On the way out he asked the junior coach if they needed help with the under-twelves.

qa.q: What did Jomon do with his team jersey?
qa.a: He turned it inside out and stuffed it at the back of the cupboard.

qa.q: Why did Jomon tell Ishita he was fine and hang up in week one?
qa.a: He was too raw with grief to talk and wanted to shut out the loss of his future.

qa.q: What helped Jomon move from hiding to grieving?
qa.a: Ishita coming anyway and listening without trying to fix things gave him space to cry and talk.

qa.q: How might the under-twelves be affected if Jomon helps coach?
qa.a: They would gain a skilled, dedicated coach who knows the game deeply.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult processing the loss of an idealised sporting future over several weeks.
